tier_reason: The README table (written by the flake.nix `bench` app) does compare against cmark and cmark-gfm, but in flake.nix only the cmark and cmark-gfm commands run through a generated /bin/sh wrapper script (`exec cmark "$@" > /dev/null`) while zigmark, lowdown and discount are spawned directly by `hyperfine -N`, so each baseline run pays an extra shell start-up on a 2-5 ms start-up-dominated workload; the C tools measured without the wrapper (lowdown 2.2 ms, discount 2.7 ms) tie or beat zigmark ReleaseFast (2.4 ms), so no valid measured win over C remains (hop start-up-dominated and AssemblyScript crippled-baseline precedents). Even taken at face value it would be C: no CPU, no baseline build flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Performance table (last updated 2026-06-04, input README.md 27 KB, hyperfine -N, 50 warm-ups, 500 runs), mean ms: lowdown 2.2 +/- 0.8, zigmark ReleaseFast 2.4 +/- 1.0, discount 2.7 +/- 1.2, zigmark ReleaseSmall 2.9 +/- 0.7, zigmark ReleaseSafe 4.4 +/- 1.0, cmark 5.3 +/- 1.4, cmark-gfm 5.6 +/- 1.2; pandoc 185.4 +/- 32.2 (separate 20-run hyperfine call). zigmark ReleaseFast vs cmark about 2.2x and vs cmark-gfm about 2.3x, ReleaseSafe vs cmark about 1.2x (derived from page data), but the cmark and cmark-gfm rows include an extra /bin/sh wrapper process that the zigmark rows do not (see caveats). lowdown (C) is faster than every zigmark build and discount (C) is within one standard deviation of ReleaseFast. Peak RSS (GNU time -v, one run each): zigmark ReleaseSmall 1952 KB, discount 2124 KB, zigmark ReleaseFast 2412 KB, lowdown 2988 KB, zigmark ReleaseSafe 3116 KB, cmark-gfm 4300 KB, cmark 4336 KB, pandoc 129416 KB; the cmark and cmark-gfm RSS figures are also taken through the shell wrapper, so they include the shell's footprint.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: zigmark: Zig 0.16.0, built by the flake's mkZigmark helper with -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, ReleaseSmall and ReleaseSafe. cmark, cmark-gfm, discount, lowdown and pandoc are the nixpkgs packages pulled in as runtimeInputs of the `bench` app in flake.nix; their versions and build flags are not stated. Harness: hyperfine -N --warmup 50 --runs 500; cmark and cmark-gfm are invoked through a generated `#!/bin/sh` script that execs them with stdout redirected to /dev/null, while zigmark, discount and lowdown are invoked directly with -o /dev/null.
corrections.workload: Convert the repository's own 27 KB README.md from Markdown to HTML on the command line, one process per run (the bench app uses the CommonMark spec.txt only when it is cached, and the published table says README.md); hyperfine -N mean wall time per process over 500 runs after 50 warm-ups, plus one-run peak RSS via GNU time -v (`nix run .#bench`, defined in flake.nix).
corrections.caveats: Harness asymmetry: in flake.nix the cmark and cmark-gfm commands are run through a generated /bin/sh wrapper (`exec cmark "$@" > /dev/null`) because cmark has no -o option, while zigmark, lowdown and discount are spawned directly by hyperfine -N; every baseline run therefore pays an extra shell start-up (about 1 ms per spawn with dash in the verifier's container; NixOS's /bin/sh is bash, which is heavier), on runs that take 2 to 5 ms in total, and hyperfine's --output=null would have avoided it. The same wrapper means the cmark and cmark-gfm peak-RSS figures are the maximum of the shell and cmark, since Linux carries the pre-exec high-water mark into ru_maxrss. One 27 KB input, so process times are dominated by start-up and file I/O; no CPU or machine stated; baseline versions and flags not stated (nixpkgs packages). C tools measured without the wrapper (lowdown 2.2 ms, discount 2.7 ms) tie or beat zigmark ReleaseFast (2.4 +/- 1.0 ms). Different parser design (mecha parser combinators) from cmark, so this is not a language-level comparison. Benchmark output is auto-written into the README by the repo's own bench app. The PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 licence forbids commercial use, so the code is reference-only.
corrections.why_faster: Not established: the apparent margin over cmark and cmark-gfm is partly a harness artefact (only their rows run through a /bin/sh wrapper), and the unwrapped C tools lowdown and discount are as fast or faster; zigmark uses a different parser design (mecha parser combinators), so any remaining difference is design, not language.

notes: Numbers on the page match the record, but flake.nix's bench app wraps only cmark and cmark-gfm in a /bin/sh exec script, so their time and RSS rows include an extra shell process on a start-up-dominated 2-5 ms workload; the unwrapped C tools (lowdown, discount) show zigmark is not faster than C. Downgraded C to D under the hop and crippled-baseline precedents; metadata (PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0, 6 stars, last commit 2026-08-07, active) checked and unchanged. If the orchestrator prefers to keep the numbers, the fallback is tier C with this harness flaw as the shortcoming.

tier_reason: Public benchmark code (bench/baselines.c, bench/ksw2_baseline.c, bench/gen.py, the bitdp-bench build step, reproduction commands in bench/README.md), compilers and flags (Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast with -Dcpu=znver4 or -Dcpu=x86_64_v3; gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native for the C harnesses) and CPU (Ryzen 7 8840U) are all stated in bench/RESULTS.md, and every tool's total cost is cross-checked; the README's headline numbers (35.2 vs 21.7 / 2.2 / 5.2 GCUPS, 15 % over edlib on real reads, 0.30 s vs 13.3 s) appear in RESULTS.md.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: bitdp: Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, built twice: -Dcpu=znver4 (AVX-512, 8 lanes of 64 bits) and -Dcpu=x86_64_v3 (AVX2, 4 lanes). Baseline harnesses built with gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native: bench/baselines.c linked against the Ubuntu packages parasail 2.6.2 and edlib 1.2.7 (the libraries themselves are distro builds, their compile flags are not stated, and the Ubuntu parasail has no AVX-512 kernels), and bench/ksw2_baseline.c compiled together with ksw2 commit 289609b (ksw_extz2_sse, 128-bit SSE). BGSA from its repository at commit dffcf9e (2022-02-24), kernels from its own generator, built with make cc=gcc.
corrections.claimed_speedup: bench/RESULTS.md (medians of three runs, GCUPS, one core): on 5,000 random 1 kbp pairs at 15 % divergence, edit distance, batched bitdp 35.20 (4 lanes AVX2) and 34.89 (8 lanes AVX-512) vs edlib 21.73, ksw2 extz2_sse 2.20, parasail scan16 5.19 and diag16 1.98; on 100,000 150 bp pairs at 10 %, batched AVX2 7.75 vs edlib 6.19 (single-pair bitdp 5.69 is slower than edlib); on 193,660 real 100 bp Illumina reads, batched AVX2 5.09 vs edlib 4.42 (about 15 %), ksw2 1.44, parasail scan16 1.57; tstv and bitpal schemes 2.3-9x ahead of ksw2 and parasail scan16. BLOSUM62 protein: bitdp 0.77-0.82 vs parasail scan16 2.87 and diag16 2.19, so several times slower. Against BGSA, the C++ tool that runs Myers' and BitPAl's hand-derived kernels in the same one-alignment-per-lane setting: edit distance 0.73-0.93x of BGSA with AVX2 and 0.90-1.20x with AVX-512, BitPAl (2,-3,-5) ties or beats BGSA's non-packed kernel (8.6 vs 8.6, 11.7 vs 9.2) and trails its packed one (8.6 vs 13.0, 11.7 vs 14.0). CRISPR-style scan of E. coli K-12 with 32 guides: 0.30 s (AVX-512) vs 13.3 s for the repo's own plain scalar reference DP, which is a correctness check, not an optimised C/C++ aligner.
corrections.caveats: Single author, single machine (Ryzen 7 8840U under WSL2). The comparison is batched SIMD lanes (one alignment per lane) against single-pair tools, a different regime from edlib's per-pair banded algorithm; on 150 bp pairs a single bitdp pair is slower than edlib. Against BGSA, the closest same-regime tool (C++, hand-derived kernels), bitdp reaches only 0.73-1.20 of its speed for edit distance and trails BGSA's packed BitPAl, so the win over C/C++ comes from batching and the derived kernel, not from Zig. edlib and parasail are Ubuntu package builds, not rebuilt at -O3 -march=native; parasail's NW kernels are affine-gap kernels run with open = extend for linear gaps. parasail's striped kernels were excluded because they returned wrong costs on some pairs (426 of 100,000 on the 150 bp edit set). The 13.3 s genome-scan figure is the repo's own scalar reference loop. Research code, API not stable.
corrections.why_faster: Bit-parallel kernel derived at compile time from the recurrence (14 word operations per column for unit edit costs versus 15 for Myers) with one alignment per SIMD lane for independent pairs; the gain over edlib, ksw2 and parasail is algorithmic and from batching, not from Zig, and against BGSA's hand-derived C++ kernels in the same batched regime bitdp is 0.73-1.20x.

tier_reason: docs/BENCHMARK.md compares against llama.cpp build 30af6e2 on the same GGUF files and thread counts, with public harness code (tools/bench_gate.py paired gate driving llama-bench -ngl 0; tools/fetch_refs.sh pins llama.cpp and builds it with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF), Fucina built with Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast native, verified x86 GGML flags, and named CPUs (Apple M1 Max, Intel i9-13950HX); the headline numbers in the record appear on the page.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Fucina: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast with the default native target (no -Dtarget); off macOS the default is -Dblas=none, on macOS the default build uses Accelerate CBLAS for f32 GEMMs at m >= 16. llama.cpp: build 30af6e2 pinned in tools/fetch_refs.sh, whose --build step runs cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF (CPU-only, Accelerate BLAS left on under macOS). The x86 llama-bench build was verified as GGML_BLAS=OFF, GGML_NATIVE=ON (-march=native), GGML_LLAMAFILE=ON, GGML_CPU_REPACK=ON, GGML_OPENMP=ON, but its binary reported build_commit unknown; the x86 leg of another record says both engines were compiled on the box with gcc-12 / zig native. The C/C++ compiler for the M1 llama.cpp build is not stated.
corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/BENCHMARK.md (snapshot 2026-07-04, updates 2026-07-10), ratio = Fucina / llama.cpp tok/s. Apple M1 Max, 8 threads: of 236 sweep cells Fucina faster in 221, parity 13, llama.cpp faster 2; dense prefill per-format geomeans 1.18-1.81x (Qwen3 0.6B seven formats and 1.7B; Qwen3.5-0.8B 1.07x on 4 lengths); Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE prefill pp64-256 1.44-2.09x; dense decode Q4_K_M/Q4_K_S +15 %, Q8_0 +14 %. Intel i9-13950HX (AVX2 + AVX-VNNI, no BLAS either side): dense Qwen3-0.6B paired-gate median ratios 1.32-1.95 per quantized format (maxima up to 2.56); 2026-07-10 dispatch fix took x86 dense decode Q5_K_M to 1.016, Q5_K_S 1.055, Q6_K 1.057; 30B MoE mid-batch pp15-33 moved from 0.36-0.52x to Q5_K_M 1.15-1.22x and Q6_K 0.97-1.05x. llama.cpp wins or open gaps: Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 pp32 0.86x, 30B Q6_K decode 0.88x on M1 (no page-cache prewarm), MoE decode 0.87-0.95x on M1 and 0.971-0.972x on x86, Q6_K 30B pp31-33 0.965-0.987x and pp64-256 0.93-0.97x on x86, Gemma-4-26B pp1-9 0.85-0.99x on x86, Gemma-4-26B mid-batch prefill on M1 0.72-0.91x cool (listed as an open gap, while the scoreboard reports 1.17-2.15x from a session in which llama.cpp ran below its own best values), and pp256 with Q4_K-transcoded experts about 15-17 % behind.
corrections.caveats: Author-run, first-party record with one dated snapshot (2026-07-04) against a pinned llama.cpp build, so results age as llama.cpp advances. On the M1 llama.cpp's Accelerate/AMX path switches on at batch >= 32 and the document says that transition costs it heavily at pp32-129 (up to 7.2x at f16 pp32), so part of the prefill win is a llama.cpp threshold effect; Fucina's own macOS default build also routes f32 GEMMs at m >= 16 to Accelerate, so the M1 rows are not BLAS-free on either side (the x86 rows are). Gemma-4 and Qwen3.5 M1 rows use best-of Fucina numbers (flagged by the author as favourable to Fucina), and the Gemma mid-batch session had llama.cpp below its strongest recorded values; the same document lists Gemma-4-26B mid-batch prefill on M1 as an open gap at 0.72-0.91x cool, contradicting the scoreboard's 1.17-2.15x. The x86 llama-bench binary reported build_commit unknown, so its commit rests on the recorded build flags. Laptop thermals and page cache move results by several percent; some cells are same-day reruns after a 2026-07-10 scheduler fix. Fucina's loops include logits/sampler work llama-bench skips (biases against Fucina). Different kernels and scheduling from ggml, so this is not a Zig-versus-C++ language comparison. tools/gen_optim_goldens.py is under CC-BY-NC-4.0 (rest MIT).
